title: Regret Aversion
description: We avoid making a decision because we fear feeling regret if it turns out badly—even when the rational choice is to act.
shortDescription: We avoid making a decision because we fear feeling regret if it turns out badly—even when the rational choice is to act.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: We avoid making a decision because we fear feeling regret if it turns out badly—even when the rational choice is to act.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: You don’t sell a losing stock because you can’t bear to lock in the loss and then watch it possibly recover. So you hold it as it drops further.
You don’t ask someone out because the imagined rejection feels worse than never knowing.
A manager doesn’t fire an underperforming employee because she imagines the awkward conversation and potential guilt.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Holding onto losers (stocks, relationships, jobs) to avoid the pain of “realizing” the loss.
Keeping options open unnecessarily, even at a cost, to avoid future “what if” thoughts.
Doing the safer, less optimal thing to minimize potential bad feelings later.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I’d hate myself if I sold and then it went up.”
“What if I make the wrong call?”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: Your decision is driven by imagining how you’ll feel after, not by expected value.
You’re not just risk‑averse; you’re specifically afraid of self‑blame.
You take a suboptimal option because it provides “emotional insurance.”

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Regret is a powerful negative emotion. The brain anticipates it and steers away from actions that could produce it, even if those actions are statistically superior. Omission (doing nothing) feels less regrettable than a commission that fails.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Recognize that regret from inaction can be as strong or stronger in the long run.
Use decision rules agreed upon in a “cold” state to override fear of regret.
Ask: “Looking back from 10 years, will I regret not acting?” The answer often shifts.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Over‑valuing “no regrets” as a life philosophy, leading to missed opportunities.
Thinking regret aversion is rational caution; it’s emotional caution that can be irrational.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: An investor buys shares at $50. They drop to $20. He refuses to sell, even though the company is failing, because selling would make him feel like a fool if they somehow rebound. The shares go to zero, and he loses everything. The fear of regret caused a total loss.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The decision you’re proud of later is often the one that felt scary at the time. Regret‑proof your future by acting now, not by hiding from the chance of a bad outcome.
